L25: # Our History
L26: 
L27: 1994
L28: 
L29: ESRB founded by the 【23†Interactive Digital Software Association†www.theesa.com】 (IDSA was renamed Entertainment Software Association in 2004)
L30: 
L31: New ESRB rating system announced, with 5 rating categories and 17 content descriptors

L35: 1995
L36: 
L37: Advertising Code of Conduct created and adopted by the IDSA
L38: 
L39: 1997
L40: 
L41: ESRB rating system established for websites, with 5 rating categories and 22 content descriptors
L42: Online Rating Notice established to warn consumers of user-generated content in online-enabled games and on websites
L43: 
L44: 1998
L45: 
L46: K-A (Kids to Adults) rating category changed to E (Everyone)

L48: 【29†Image】

L51: 
L52: First ESRB Public Service Announcements launched featuring Tiger Woods, Derek Jeter and Regis Philbin

L55: 
L56: 【30†Image】 【31†Image】 【32†Image】 【33†Image】 【34†Image】

L58: 2000
L59: Advertising Review Council established as division of ESRB to monitor compliance with industry-adopted marketing and advertising guidelines
L60: 
L61: ESRB 【5†enforcement system】 established to impose sanctions, including points, fines and corrective actions, on companies who do not comply with ESRB rules and guidelines
L62: 
L63: 2001
L64: 
L65: New target marketing guidelines for Mature-rated games introduced
L66: 【35†ESRB Privacy Online†www.esrbprivacy.org】 certification service launched and sanctioned by the FTC as a “Safe Harbor” under COPPA
L67: 
L68: 2002
L69: 
L70: Arthur Pober departs as ESRB’s founding president; Patricia Vance joins ESRB as its new president
L71: 
L72: 2003
L73: 
L74: ESRB rating system for websites discontinued
L75: 
L76: 2005
L77: 
L78: E10+ rating category introduced for games that may be suitable for ages 10 and older
L79: 
L80: 【36†Image】

L82: 2006
L83: 
L84: ESRB increases fine up to $1 million for non-disclosure of pertinent content
L85: 【37†ESRB Retail Council (ERC)】 launched by ESRB and leading computer and video game retailers; “ERC Commitment to Parents” is adopted by all ERC retail members
L86: 
L87: National radio and TV PSA 【38†campaign】 promoting ratings awareness launched with U.S. Senators Hillary Rodham Clinton and Joseph Lieberman
L88: 
L89: ESRB launches its first PSA campaign featuring artwork by Penny Arcade
L90: 
L91: 2008
L92: The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) finds eight in ten underage buyers are turned away when attempting to purchase Mature-rated games
L93: 
L94: PTA and ESRB release “Parents Guide to Video Games, Parental Controls and Online Safety”
L95: 
L96: Rating summaries are introduced along with ESRB’s mobile website
L97: 
L98: 2009
L99: 
L100: ESRB Privacy Online launches E.U. Privacy Seal Certification program
L101: The FTC’s 【39†sixth follow-up Report to Congress†www.ftc.gov】 lauds ESRB for having “the strongest self-regulatory code” and confirms that retailers have maintained their 80% store policy compliance rate
L102: 
L103: 2010
L104: 
L105: ESRB launches PSA campaigns with the 【40†New Orleans Saints】 and 【41†Chicago Blackhawks】, both of which include TV and radio ads running in their respective regions as well as in-stadium/arena
L106: The ESRB Website Council (EWC) is established to help ensure that game enthusiast sites post complete rating information and employ age-gates on trailers and videos for M- and AO-rated games
L107: 
L108: 2011
L109: 
L110: The FTC’s 【42†mystery shopper study†www.ftc.gov】 finds enforcement of entertainment ratings to be “highest among video game sellers” with 87% overall compliance
L111: 
L112: ESRB introduces an 【43†automated, streamlined process】 for assigning ratings to console downloadable games
L113: The U.S. Supreme Court rules in 【44†Brown v. EMA/ESA†www.theesa.com】 that video games qualify for First Amendment protection and the sale of violent games may not be restricted by law, a landmark decision that recognized the effectiveness of the ESRB rating system
L114: 
L115: ESRB is 【45†commissioned】 by the CTIA, the trade association representing wireless carriers in the U.S., to develop and administer a rating system for mobile apps
L116: ESRB launches TV, radio and in-arena PSA campaign with the 【46†Washington Capitals】
L117: 
L118: 2012
L119: 
L120: ESRB releases a new 【47†print and online PSA campaign】 featuring real-life parents and gamers and artwork by Penny Arcade
L121: 
L122: ESRB launches TV and radio PSA campaign with the 【48†San Francisco Giants】 with airings in AT&T Park and throughout the Bay Area during the 2012 MLB season
L123: 
L124: 【49†Interactive Elements】 added to ESRB ratings for digital games and apps
L125: ESRB introduces a 【43†digital rating service】 to provide cost-free ratings for digitally delivered games
L126: 
L127: 2013
L128: 
L129: The FTC announces that 【50†video game retailers】 continue to have the highest level of store policy enforcement as compared to other entertainment retailers with 87% overall compliance
L130: 
L131: ESRB’s Safe Harbor privacy program is re-branded 【2†ESRB Privacy Certified】 featuring new seals and privacy resources for existing and new members
L132: 
L133: 【51†Image】
L134: 【52†International Age Rating Coalition (IARC)†www.globalratings.com】 is incorporated
L135: 
L136: 2014
L137: 
L138: International Age Rating Coalition (IARC) begins assigning ratings to games and apps on Mozilla’s Firefox Marketplace
L139: 
L140: 2015
L141: 
L142: The Australian Classification Board (ACB) becomes an IARC participating rating authority
L143: 
L144: The Nintendo eShop deploys the IARC rating system for all digitally delivered video games and apps
L145: Google Play deploys the IARC rating system, resulting in the display of ESRB ratings for all apps available in North America
L146: 
L147: 2016
L148: 
L149: The Windows Store deploys the IARC rating system for all digitally delivered games and apps
L150: 
L151: 2017
L152: 
L153: The Oculus Store 【53†deploys†developer.oculus.com】 the IARC rating system for all VR games and apps
L154: 
L155: Republic of Korea’s 【54†Game Rating and Administration Committee (GRAC)】 becomes the newest participant in the IARC rating system
L156: 
L157: 2018
L158: 【55†ESRB begins assigning】 【4†Interactive Elements】 to physical (e.g., boxed) games, including In-Game Purchases and Users Interact
L159: 
L160: PlayStation deploys IARC on the PlayStation Store to display ESRB ratings for all digitally delivered games, including for PlayStation VR
L161: 
L162: 2019
L163: 
L164: ESRB and Penny Arcade launch their third PSA campaign, featuring both artwork and voiceover from the Penny Arcade team
L165: 
L166: 【56†Origin†www.origin.com】 deploys the IARC rating system for all digitally delivered games
L167: 
L168: 2020
L169: ESRB 【57†introduces】 In-Game Purchases (Includes Random Items) 【4†Interactive Element】
L170: 
L171: 
L172: 
L173: 2021
L174: 
L175: ESRB launches 【12†¡Vamos a Jugar!】 (or “Let’s Play” in English) to help Spanish-speaking parents and guardians learn about the ESRB rating system, parental controls, and more
L176: 
L177: Google Stadia deploys the IARC rating system for all digitally delivered video games
L178: ESRB introduces the RATING PENDING – LIKELY MATURE 17+ 【4†notice】 that publishers can include in advertisements and promotional materials for upcoming video games that have not yet been rated but are anticipated to be rated Mature 17+
L179: 
L180: 2022
L181: 
L182: Amazon Luna deploys the IARC rating system for its cloud gaming platform.
L183: 
L184: Pico deploys the IARC rating system for its VR games and experiences.
L185: ESRB launches 【10†The Family Gaming Guide】, a new resource to help parents manage their kids’ video game experiences and keep peace of mind
L186: 
L187: 2023
L188: 
L189: Epic Games Store deploys the IARC rating system for its games.
L190: 
L191: The International Age Rating Coalition (IARC) celebrates its 10th anniversary.
L192: 
L193: 2024
L194: 
L195: One Store deploys the IARC rating system for its games and apps.
L196: ESRB celebrates its 30th anniversary with “【58†E is For Everyone†www.youtube.com】,” an original song and animated music video featuring many ESRB employees.
L197: 
L198: 2025
L199: 
L200: Taiwan’s Digital Game Self-regulation Committee becomes the newest participant in the IARC rating system.
L201: 
L202: Fortnite deploys the IARC rating system for its games and experiences.
L203: 
L204: ESRB president, Patricia Vance, accepts the 【59†Visionary Award†gamesbeat.com】 at the 2025 GamesBeat Summit.
L205: Facebook Gaming deploys the IARC rating system for its games.
L206: 
L207: ESRB launches the 【60†Level Up: Talkin’ Ratings】 outreach initiative; a series of 【61†videos†www.youtube.com】 and blogs offering information and tips for parents about the rating system and creating appropriate video game experiences for kids.
L208: 
L209: 2026
L210: 
L211: Indonesia’s Indonesia Game Rating System (IGRS) becomes the newest participant in the IARC rating system.
L212: Saudi Arabia’s General Authority for Media Regulation (Gmedia) becomes the newest participant in the IARC rating system.
L213: ### Did You Know?
L214: 
L215: 65% of the ESRB ratings assigned to physical and console downloadable video games in 2024 were either E (Everyone) or E10+ (Everyone 10+).
L216: 
L217: 【62†Learn More on our Blog】

L219: ### Did You Know?
L220: 
L221: 83% of parents with kids who play video games are aware of ESRB ratings and 77% regularly check them before buying a game. (Source: Hart Research Associates, 2025)
L222: 
L223: 【63†Learn More on our Blog】
L224: ### Did You Know?
L225: 
L226: Most parents consider each part (Rating Category, Content Descriptors, Interactive Elements) of the ESRB rating system to be either “very” or “extremely” important when deciding if a game or app is appropriate for their kids. (Source: Hart Research Associates, 2025)
L227:

L231: 
L232: Industry guidelines, which are enforced by the ESRB, prohibit the inappropriate target marketing of Mature-rated games.
L233: 
L234: 【64†Learn More about Principles and Guidelines】
L235: ### Did You Know?
L236: 
L237: ESRB has an enforcement system which allows for the imposition of sanctions, fines (including fines up to $1 million), and corrective actions on publishers for non-compliance with its guidelines.
L238: 
L239: 【5†Learn More about Rating Process】
L240: 
L241: ### Did You Know?
L242: 
L243: According to the U.S. 【65†Federal Trade Commission†www.ftc.gov】 87% of kids under the age of 17 are turned away when trying to buy an M-rated game at retail.
L244: 
L245: 【66†Learn More on our Blog】
L246: ### Did You Know?
L247: 
L248: The late U.S. Supreme Court Justice Antonin Scalia wrote: “This [ESRB rating] system does much to ensure that minors cannot purchase seriously violent games on their own, and that parents who care about the matter can readily evaluate the games their children bring home.”
L249: 
L250: 【67†Learn More at supremecourt.gov†www.supremecourt.gov】
L251: 
L252: ### Did You Know?
L253: 
L254: The E (Everyone) rating was originally called K-A (Kids to Adults) but was changed in 1998.
L255: 
L256: 【16†Learn More in History of ESRB】
L257: ### Did You Know?
L258: 
L259: The ESRB rating system has three parts – Rating Categories, Content Descriptors and Interactive Elements, the latter of which were introduced in 2013.
L260: 
L261: 【4†Learn More on Ratings Guide】
L262: 
L263: ### Did You Know?
L264: 
L265: Introduced in 2008, Rating Summaries provide greater detail about the content in physical games rated by the ESRB, and are exclusively available on this website or the ESRB mobile app by conducting a title search.
L266: 
L267: 【4†Learn More on Ratings Guide】
L268: ### Did You Know?
L269: 
L270: ESRB uses more than 30 different Content Descriptors to help communicate what’s in a game.
L271: 
L272: 【4†Learn More on Ratings Guide】
L273: 
L274: ### Did You Know?
L275: 
L276: The FTC considers the ESRB to have “the strongest self-regulatory code” among media rating systems in the U.S. and has confirmed that retailers maintain a high store policy compliance rate.
L277: 
L278: 【66†Learn More on our Blog】
L279: ### Did You Know?
L280: 
L281: Founded in 2013 by many of the world’s leading video game rating authorities, the International Age Rating Coalition (IARC) administers the first globally streamlined age classification process for digital games and mobile apps that respects the unique cultural norms of each region.
L282: 
L283: 【52†Learn More at globalratings.com†www.globalratings.com】
L284: ### Did You Know?
L285: 
L286: In 1999 ESRB Privacy Online (now called ESRB Privacy Certified) launched its certification program and was sanctioned by the FTC as a “Safe Harbor” under 【68†Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act†www.ftc.gov】 (COPPA).
L287:

L291: 
L292: More than 67% of parents would be more comfortable allowing their children to download and play a game certified by ESRB Privacy Certified (Source: Hart Research Associates, 2024).
L293: 
L294: 【2†Learn More on privacy】

L296: 
L297: It’s never too late to have “the conversation” with your kids about what, when, and how they can play!
L298: 
L299: 【10†Learn More on Family gaming guide】

L302: 
L303: Activating parental controls on your children’s video game devices helps you enforce house rules, such as limiting play time, blocking games with certain ESRB ratings, and managing in-game spending.
L304: 
L305: 【9†Learn More on Parental controls】
